claims.text: Baseline TiVNbTa is a single-phase BCC dendritic alloy.
Baseline TiVNbTa has about 800 MPa yield strength and approximately 40% strain at room temperature.
Baseline TiVNbTa has 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 1273 K.
The intervention is to add approximately 5–10 at.% W to TiVNbTa.
Adding 5–10 at.% W will increase the high-temperature yield and compressive strengths of TiVNbTa.
W addition will stabilize the BCC matrix of TiVNbTa.
W atoms will act as solid-solution strengthening solutes in the BCC matrix.
W addition may produce fine strengthening precipitates in TiVNbTa.
Solid-solution strengthening of a BCC matrix and hard precipitates can increase compressive strength in a Ta- and W-containing HEA.
W addition will reduce atomic mobility at elevated temperature and thereby improve resistance to softening.
The cited evidence reports analogous strengthening effects in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW.
The modified alloy will have yield strength notably above 330 MPa and compressive strength notably above 423 MPa at 1273 K.
The modified alloy will retain room-temperature ductility near the baseline value of 40% strain.
The proposed alloy will maintain thermal compatibility with W and CuCrZr.
W and CuCrZr have an operating-temperature gap that motivates an intermediate layer.
The relevant elevated-temperature testing boundary is approximately 1273 K at strains up to 30–40%.
A controlled comparison will use TiVNbTa alloys containing 0, 5, and 10 at.% W under identical processing conditions.
XRD, TEM, and SEM will be used to assess phase stability and precipitate formation.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant strength increase at 1273 K will falsify the performance prediction.
Marked ductility loss or an unwanted phase transformation would by itself falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed strengthening mechanism.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis predicts no significant loss of room-temperature ductility, whereas the uncertainty field acknowledges possible brittleness; this is framed as uncertainty rather than a direct logical contradiction, but it materially qualifies the confident prediction.

The alloy is described as having a stabilized BCC matrix while also possibly containing strengthening precipitates. If those precipitates constitute a distinct phase, the modified alloy would not remain strictly single-phase BCC.
